title: Poem 1 — Corona Says (Vishnu S. Rai)
notes:
## The poem at a glance

"Corona Says" by Vishnu S. Rai is a poem of the pandemic told from an outrageous point of view: the virus itself is given the microphone. The speaker is Corona — personified, courteous, faintly wounded at being called a monster — and the poem is its defence and its lecture. The device that makes everything else possible is **personification**, and Rai pushes it further than a mask: the virus has a voice, a grievance and a moral argument. The result is satire with a stethoscope: humanity is put on trial, and the accused is asked to defend the earth.

## Reading it closely, movement by movement

The poem opens with the virus answering its own reputation. It does not deny the deaths — it refuses the monopoly of blame: humans have slaughtered each other and the planet for centuries, and no one called *them* a virus. The **tone** here is the poem's tightrope: polite, reasonable, faintly sarcastic — the calm of a lawyer who knows the evidence is on its side. Listen to the irony: the deadliest visitor in modern history speaking in the language of a polite dinner guest.

Then the indictment, and it is environmental. Corona points at what humans do daily — the felled forests, the poisoned rivers, the caged animals, the wars — and asks which species deserves the name of pest. The **irony** is structural now, not just tonal: the creature that "locked the world indoors" claims it merely gave humans a taste of their own medicine — the cages they build, the confinement they impose.

The close turns the mirror fully around: the virus claims that during lockdown, when humans were shut in, the earth healed — skies cleared, rivers ran cleaner, animals walked streets that had been stolen from them. Whether the claim is scientifically neat or not, the **argument of the poem** is: the earth was better off with humans confined, which is the most uncomfortable sentence in the NEB syllabus — and the reason the poem is taught.

## The devices, with evidence

- **Personification** — the master key: the virus speaks, argues, feels wronged. Every other device grows from this choice.
- **Irony (verbal and situational)** — a killer pleads for peace; the "monster" accuses humanity of monstrosity; the cure for the earth is the disease of the people.
- **Satire** — the poem is an organised attack on human arrogance, dressed as a virus's self-defence.
- **Rhetorical questions** — the virus cross-examines; the questions are the cage bars of the trial.
- **Allusion** — wars, hunting, pollution: the poem gestures at history's real crimes without listing dates.
- **Tone** — mock-politeness throughout; the danger is in the courtesy, not the threat.

The exam question "why has the poet given the virus a voice?" is answered by all of the above at once: the personification forces the reader to hear the accused planet speak, and hearing it is the poem's whole point.

## The themes worth an essay

**Human arrogance and nature's revenge** — the central theme: we named the virus the invader; the poem insists we were the invaders first. **Environmental justice** — the lockdown clearing of skies is read as evidence of what the earth wants. **The relativity of blame** — every species is a pest from some other's point of view; the word "pest" is a position, not a fact. And beneath all three, **humility**: the poem asks for a smaller human ego, not a smaller human population — the difference matters and the exam rewards noticing it.

## The title, defended

"Corona Says" — three words that carry the whole device. Not "About Corona", not "The Pandemic": *says*. The title promises a speaking subject, and delivers a speaker nobody wanted to hear from. The justification a candidate should write: the title hands the microphone to the least popular witness, and the poem is that testimony.

## How NEB asks it

**"Why does the speaker call humans the real virus?" (2–4 marks)** — the environmental indictment: our daily destruction outdoes its accident. **"What happened to nature during the lockdown, according to the poem?"** — skies cleared, rivers cleaned, animals reclaimed space: the earth healed when humans paused. **"Do you agree with the poem's view? Give reasons."** — the dialectic frame: concede the discomfort, weigh the exaggeration, land on the legitimate kernel (human arrogance is real; the poem overstates for effect — that is what satire does). **Short answer: "What is the tone of the poem?"** — mock-polite, ironic, satirical: courtesy carrying a charge.

One last habit for this poem and every satirical text: never answer the surface question ("is the virus right?") without naming the device ("the virus is a *device* — a personification that lets the poet put humanity on trial"). That sentence, written early, is the difference between an opinion and an answer.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: The poem personifies CORONAVIRUS as a speaker defending itself — the reversal (virus accusing humans) is the poem's central irony; state it first.
Trick 2: The virus's argument: humans destroyed nature and each other; the pandemic only balanced the scales — collect two lines supporting this accusation.
Trick 3: Message questions: humility before nature and reflection during lockdown — connect one image (empty roads, clear skies) to the message.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does the speaker (corona) claim humans deserved the pandemic? (2 marks) — humans exploited nature and waged wars; corona presents itself as nature's correction.
Q. What positive changes does the poem note during lockdown? (2 marks) — cleaner air, family time, reflection on priorities.
keyPoints: The virus speaks — personification lets corona accuse humans of destroying nature.
Central message: the pandemic was nature's warning; humans must change, not just survive.
